## Brachistochrone — Complete Derivation

**Setup and coordinates.** Place the origin at the starting point $(0,0)$ and take the $y$-axis pointing **downward** (so the endpoint is $(a,b)$ with $b>0$). The bead is released from rest and slides without friction under gravity $g$.

**Step 1 — Speed from energy conservation.** Starting from rest at $y=0$, conservation of mechanical energy gives
$$\tfrac12 m v^2 = mgy \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v(y)=\sqrt{2gy}.$$

**Step 2 — Functional to minimize.** With $ds=\sqrt{1+y'^2}\,dx$ and $v=\sqrt{2gy}$, the total descent time is
$$T[y]=\int_0^a \frac{\sqrt{1+y'^2}}{\sqrt{2gy}}\,dx,\qquad y'=\frac{dy}{dx}.$$
The integrand (the Lagrangian) is
$$L(y,y')=\frac{\sqrt{1+y'^2}}{\sqrt{2gy}}.$$

**Step 3 — First integral (Beltrami identity).** Since $L$ has no explicit $x$-dependence, the Beltrami identity gives a first integral:
$$L - y'\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}=\text{const}.$$
Computing
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}=\frac{y'}{\sqrt{2gy}\,\sqrt{1+y'^2}},$$
we obtain
$$L-y'\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}=\frac{\sqrt{1+y'^2}}{\sqrt{2gy}}-\frac{y'^2}{\sqrt{2gy}\,\sqrt{1+y'^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2gy}\,\sqrt{1+y'^2}}=\text{const}.$$
Squaring and absorbing all constants into a single positive constant $2k$,
$$\boxed{\,y\,(1+y'^2)=2k\,}\qquad(k>0).$$

**Step 4 — Parametrize the extremal.** Rewrite as
$$y'^2=\frac{2k-y}{y}.$$
Introduce the parameter $\theta$ via
$$y=k(1-\cos\theta).$$
Then $2k-y=k(1+\cos\theta)$, so
$$y'^2=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta}=\cot^2\!\tfrac{\theta}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dy}{dx}=\cot\tfrac{\theta}{2}.$$
Since $dy/d\theta=k\sin\theta$,
$$\frac{dx}{d\theta}=\frac{dy/d\theta}{dy/dx}=\frac{k\sin\theta}{\cot(\theta/2)}=k\sin\theta\,\tan\tfrac{\theta}{2}=2k\sin^2\!\tfrac{\theta}{2}=k(1-\cos\theta).$$
Integrating with $x(0)=0$:
$$x=k(\theta-\sin\theta).$$

**Step 5 — The minimizing curve is a cycloid.** The extremal is
$$\boxed{\;x=k(\theta-\sin\theta),\qquad y=k(1-\cos\theta)\;}$$
which is a **cycloid**: the trajectory of a point on the rim of a circle of radius $k$ rolling along the $x$-axis. The curve has a vertical tangent (cusp) at the origin $\theta=0$, which is physically sensible — the bead starts from rest, so the optimal path drops steeply to build up speed quickly.

**Step 6 — Determine $k$ from the endpoint.** At $\theta=\theta_1$ the curve reaches $(a,b)$:
$$a=k(\theta_1-\sin\theta_1),\qquad b=k(1-\cos\theta_1).$$
Eliminating $k$,
$$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\theta_1-\sin\theta_1}{1-\cos\theta_1},$$
which fixes $\theta_1\in(0,2\pi)$, and then $k=b/(1-\cos\theta_1)$.

**Step 7 — Minimal descent time.** Substituting the parametrization into $T$:
$$\sqrt{1+y'^2}=\csc\tfrac{\theta}{2},\quad \sqrt{2gy}=2\sqrt{gk}\,\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2},\quad \frac{dx}{d\theta}=2k\sin^2\!\tfrac{\theta}{2}.$$
Hence the integrand simplifies dramatically:
$$\frac{\sqrt{1+y'^2}}{\sqrt{2gy}}\frac{dx}{d\theta}=\frac{\csc(\theta/2)}{2\sqrt{gk}\sin(\theta/2)}\cdot 2k\sin^2\!\tfrac{\theta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{g}}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\;T_{\min}=\int_0^{\theta_1}\sqrt{\frac{k}{g}}\,d\theta=\theta_1\sqrt{\frac{k}{g}}\;}.$$

**Step 8 — Why this is a (global) minimum.** The integrand $L=\sqrt{1+y'^2}/\sqrt{2gy}$ is convex in $y'$ (its second $y'$-derivative is positive), so any stationary point of the functional is a local minimizer. Moreover, among all piecewise-$C^1$ curves joining $(0,0)$ to $(a,b)$ with $y\ge 0$, the cycloid is the unique global minimizer — a classical result following from the strict convexity of $L$ in $y'$ together with the positivity of $y$ along admissible curves. No competing extremal exists (the Beltrami first integral has a unique solution family up to the single parameter $k$), and the straight-line path gives a strictly larger time, confirming the cycloid attains the infimum.

**Conclusion.** The path of fastest descent is an arc of a cycloid
$$x=k(\theta-\sin\theta),\quad y=k(1-\cos\theta),\quad 0\le\theta\le\theta_1,$$
with $k$ and $\theta_1$ fixed by the endpoint $(a,b)$, and the minimal time of descent is
$$T_{\min}=\theta_1\sqrt{k/g}.$$
